8.title: the man who argued with God about Sodom
8.hook: the man who argued with God about Sodom
8.howItsDone: Jews read Abraham's argument over Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera each autumn, and the Jewish tradition of questioning and arguing, with God and with one another, runs through the Psalms, Job and the Talmud's recorded debates.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sabbath commandment, remember and observe, even the ox resting. Your line was rest is for everyone. Did you lighten someone's load? Day eight.

An old man is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. Three visitors arrive, he feeds them, and as they leave, God tells him something. The cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, have done terrible things, and God is going to see about them. Most people in a story like this would bow, or nod, or quietly go back inside. This man doesn't. The text says he comes closer. And then he does something that surprises people when they first read it. He starts to argue. With God. Today: the first great argument in the Torah, and the man who made it.
screen: `A TENT IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `GOD SPEAKS OF SODOM.` → `ABRAHAM COMES CLOSER.`

segments.voice: Abraham. Born Abram, the text says, and renamed when God promised he'd be the father of many nations. Jews call him Avraham avinu, Abraham our father, the first to walk this path. And in Genesis eighteen, he bargains. What if there are fifty good people in the city? Will you sweep them away with the rest? Then he says the line that stands at the center of this story. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" Think about the nerve of that. He's holding God to God's own standard. And God answers: for fifty, I'll spare it. So Abraham keeps going. Forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Each time he gets more polite, and more stubborn. He even says he's "but dust and ashes." He's humble and he doesn't back down, both at once. He stops at ten. Why ten? The text doesn't say. Some teachers note that ten is the smallest number that makes a community, and we'll meet that ten again. In the end, ten good people aren't found. But the argument is never scolded. God listens to every round. That's why this story matters so much in Jewish life. Moses argues with God later. So does Job. The Psalms complain out loud. The Talmud is a library of arguments, with the losing side written down and kept. There's a Hasidic story of a rabbi who put God on trial on behalf of his people. Arguing with God, in this tradition, isn't the opposite of faith. It's one of the ways faith talks.

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one thing that seems unfair to you right now, in your life or in the world. Don't smooth it over. Say it plainly, inside. If you pray, you can say it to God the way Abraham did: direct, respectful, and not backing down. If you don't, say it honestly to yourself. The bell holds the time.

9.title: wrestling all night, limping, renamed
9.carry: you'll limp and you'll be blessed
9.howItsDone: Jews read Jacob's wrestling in the Torah portion Vayishlach each year; the name Israel, the people's name, comes from this story, and observant Jews still do not eat the sciatic nerve of an animal because of Jacob's hip.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abraham, bargaining with God from fifty down to ten. Your line was you're allowed to argue. Did you say something plainly that needed saying? Day nine.

It's the night before the hardest meeting of his life. Twenty years ago Jacob cheated his twin brother Esau out of their father's blessing and ran. Now he's coming home, and Esau is on the road with four hundred men. Jacob sends his family across a river called the Jabbok and stays behind, alone, in the dark. And then, the text says, a man wrestles with him until the break of dawn. No name. No warning. No explanation. Just two bodies in the dirt all night long. Today: the wrestler, and the name the whole people still carries.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS AFTER THE LIE.` → `ALONE AT THE RIVER.` → `A MAN WRESTLES HIM TILL DAWN.`

segments.voice: Jacob. In Hebrew, Yaakov, from the word for heel, because he was born holding on to his twin brother's heel. He's been grabbing ever since. Who is he fighting? The text calls him a man. The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. Jacob himself names the place Peniel, the face of God, because he says he saw God face to face. One old midrash says it was Esau's angel. The Torah doesn't settle it, and maybe that's the point: some nights you can't tell who you're fighting. As dawn comes, the stranger can't win, so he touches Jacob's hip and wrenches it. And Jacob, hurt, still won't let go. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The blessing is a new name. "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Israel: one who wrestles with God. Think about that. A whole people named not for someone who obeyed quietly, or never doubted, but for someone who fought all night and held on. And he doesn't walk away clean. The sun rises, and Jacob is limping. The Torah says that's why, to this day, the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, the sciatic nerve, and observant Jews still don't. A dietary law that remembers an injury. The blessing and the limp come together. He's hurt, and he's renamed, in the same morning.

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one thing you're wrestling with right now, a decision, a person, a question. Don't try to win it in the next minute. Just hold on to it, the way Jacob held on, and ask what blessing might be in it. If you pray, you can ask for that blessing. The bell holds the time.
Jacob. The heel-grabber who wrestled until dawn, came away limping, and was renamed Israel. Ninth word.

10.title: not charity
10.hook: not charity — justice; the box on the counter
10.carry: give before you feel like it
10.tomorrow: the story every Passover retells in first person
10.howItsDone: Many Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, often dropping coins in before lighting Shabbat candles; traditional Jewish law expects everyone to give, and many give a tenth of their income.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jacob, wrestling till dawn, limping, renamed Israel. Your line was you'll limp and you'll be blessed. Did something hard give you anything back? Day ten.

In a lot of Jewish kitchens there's a small tin box on the counter, often blue and white, with a slot in the top. Nobody makes a speech about it. A kid drops in a coin after finding one on the sidewalk. A grandmother drops a few in on Friday afternoon, before she lights the candles. When it's full, it goes to a food bank, a school, a family down the street. It's easy to call that charity. But the word written on the box doesn't mean charity. It means something sharper. Today: the box on the counter, and why it isn't a favor.
screen: `A TIN BOX WITH A SLOT.` → `COINS BEFORE THE CANDLES.` → `IT ISN'T CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Tzedakah comes from tzedek: justice, righteousness, what's right. Charity, in English, grows from a word for love, and love comes and goes. Tzedakah assumes something else: that part of what you have was never fully yours. It's the poor person's share, and giving it is setting things right. That's why it isn't optional in Jewish law. Everyone gives. The Talmud says that even someone who lives on tzedakah should give some. Deuteronomy says: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word there is tzedek, said twice. The rabbis asked why twice, and one answer is: pursue justice, and pursue it justly, even in how you give. In the twelfth century, the great scholar Maimonides laid out eight levels of tzedakah, like the rungs of a ladder. Near the bottom: giving, but grudgingly. Higher: giving before you're asked. Higher still: giving so that neither side knows the other, so nobody has to feel ashamed. And the top rung, above all the others: helping someone so they won't need help again. A loan, a partnership, a job. Tzedakah at its best ends the need for tzedakah. Maimonides also noticed something about us. A person who gives a thousand coins at once, he said, grows less than a person who gives one coin a thousand times, because it's the repeated act that shapes the giver. That's what the box on the counter is for. Not a feeling of generosity, waited for. A habit, built one coin at a time, until justice is just something your hands do.

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one need near you: a food bank, a neighbor, a cause you've meant to support for months. Decide on one small, specific amount, of money or of time. Not what feels generous. Just what's fair. Hold that decision until the bell ends, and then act on it before the feeling fades. The bell holds the time.
Tzedakah. Giving as justice, the poor person's share, not a favor. Tenth word.
Your line: give before you feel like it. Today, give one small thing, a coin, a donation, an hour, before you've talked yourself into it or out of it. Day ten.

11.title: the story every Passover retells in first person
11.hook: the story every Passover retells in first person
11.tomorrow: "we will do and we will hear"
11.howItsDone: At Passover, Jewish families hold a seder, reading the Haggadah around the table: the youngest asks the four questions, the story of the Exodus is told in the first person, and matzah, bitter herbs and salt water are eaten as part of the telling.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzedakah. Justice, not charity, one coin at a time. Your line was give before you feel like it. Did you give something before the feeling caught up? Day eleven.
screen: `TZEDAKAH — GIVE BEFORE YOU FEEL LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: It's a spring night, and a long table is crowded with plates that don't match, borrowed chairs, a cousin you see once a year. On the table: flat crackers, a bowl of salt water, bitter herbs, a roasted bone. The youngest child stands up, a little nervous, and asks a question in a sing-song everyone knows: why is this night different from all other nights? And the grown-ups answer. Not with "once upon a time." Not with "our ancestors." They answer with one word: we. Today: the story every Passover retells, and why it's told as if it happened to you.
screen: `A LONG TABLE, A SPRING NIGHT.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE ANSWER STARTS WITH WE.`

segments.voice: The Exodus is the going out: the story in the book of Exodus of the Israelites enslaved in Egypt, a Pharaoh who fears them, a baby in a basket who grows up to be Moses, ten plagues, a night of leaving in such a hurry the bread has no time to rise, and a sea that opens. It's the story Judaism keeps returning to more than any other. The prayers mention it every day. The Sabbath commandment remembers it, as we saw on day seven. But at Passover it isn't only remembered. It's retold, around a table, following a little book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. The Torah itself commands the telling. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me. When I came out. And so the answer to the child's question begins with a line drawn from Deuteronomy: we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. The Mishnah makes it a rule: in every generation, a person must see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Not a history lesson. A memory you're invited into. And it turns into ethics. The Torah repeats one command about the stranger more often than almost anything else: "And a stranger shalt thou not wrong, neither shalt thou oppress him; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You know what it's like, the text says. You were there. So when someone is the outsider now, remember which side of the story you were on.

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Remember a time you were the outsider: the new kid, the one who didn't speak the language, the one who didn't know the rules. Feel it again, just a little. Then think of someone who's the outsider in your life right now. Hold both of them, the old you and that person, together. The bell holds the time.
The Exodus. The going out of Egypt, retold every Passover in the first person, as if it happened to you. Eleventh word.
Your line: we were slaves. Today, do one kind thing for someone who's new, or foreign, or on the outside, because you remember what that was like. Day eleven.

12.title: "we will do and we will hear"
12.hook: "we will do and we will hear" — practice before belief
12.tomorrow: why they're called words, not commandments
12.howItsDone: Jews celebrate the giving of the Torah at Sinai on the festival of Shavuot, seven weeks after Passover; many stay up all night studying Torah, and the Ten Commandments are read aloud in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Exodus, told at the seder as if it happened to you. Your line was we were slaves. Did you do one kind thing for an outsider? Day twelve.

Three months out of Egypt, a crowd of former slaves is camped at the foot of a mountain in the desert. They've been told to wash, to wait, to keep back from the slopes. On the third morning there's thunder, lightning, a thick cloud on the peak, and the sound of a horn getting louder and louder until the whole camp is shaking. Then the covenant is read out loud to them: what this new life with God will ask. And the people give an answer, all together, that the rabbis never stopped talking about. It's two words in Hebrew, and they're in the wrong order. Today: the mountain, and the answer.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN IN THE DESERT.` → `THUNDER, CLOUD, A HORN.` → `AN ANSWER IN THE WRONG ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sinai is the mountain where, in the Torah's story, God gives the Torah to Israel. Nobody knows for certain which mountain it was, and the text isn't interested in the map. What matters is what happens there. After the laws are read, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation, the people say: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew: na'aseh v'nishma. We will do, and we will hear. Look at the order. Most of us would say it the other way round. Explain it to me first, then I'll decide whether to do it. Here the doing comes first, and the understanding follows. The Talmud tells a story about that moment: when Israel put doing before hearing, a voice from heaven asked, who revealed to my children this secret that the angels use? That's practice before belief. It's a very Jewish idea. You light the candles before you have a theory of candles. You give the coin before you feel generous, like we saw on day ten. The meaning grows out of the doing. The rabbis also argued about that day, and they wrote the argument down. One teacher said the mountain was held over the people like a barrel, as if they had no real choice. Others answered that they accepted freely, and accepted again in later generations. Both readings are kept. And there's one more teaching: that every Jewish soul, even of people not yet born, stood at Sinai. Converts, too, are said to have been there. The whole people, past and future, at the foot of one mountain. Many Jews celebrate that day every year, at the festival of Shavuot.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN WHERE TORAH IS GIVEN.` · `NA'ASEH V'NISHMA — DO, THEN HEAR.` · `THE SECRET THE ANGELS USE.` · `EVERY SOUL STOOD THERE.` · then, large: `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one good thing you've been meaning to do but keep putting off until you understand it better, or feel more ready. A call. An apology. A habit. Picture yourself doing it first, today, and letting the understanding come afterward. The bell holds the time.

Your line: do first. Today, pick one good thing you've been waiting to feel ready for, and do it before you feel ready. Day twelve.

13.title: why they're called words, not commandments
13.hook: why they're called words, not commandments
13.carry: ten sentences to build a life on
13.howItsDone: Jews read the Ten Words aloud in synagogue when they come up in the yearly Torah cycle and on the festival of Shavuot, and in many congregations everyone stands to hear them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sinai, and the answer we will do, and we will hear. Your line was do first. Did you do one thing before you felt ready? Day thirteen.

You've seen them. Two stone tablets with rounded tops, on a courthouse wall, in an old movie with a parting sea, on a poster in a classroom. The Ten Commandments. Ten rules, carved in stone. Here's the surprise. In Hebrew, the Torah never calls them that. Not once. And the very first of them, the way Jews count, isn't a commandment at all. There's no "thou shalt" in it. It doesn't tell anybody to do anything. So what is it, and why is it first? Today: the ten sentences, and why they're called words.
screen: `TWO TABLETS, ROUNDED TOPS.` → `NEVER CALLED COMMANDMENTS.` → `THE FIRST ONE ISN'T A RULE.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're aseret ha-dibrot, the ten sayings, or, as the Torah itself puts it in Exodus and Deuteronomy, the ten words. Devarim. Words, things said, things spoken to someone. Not a legal code posted on a wall. Something said, out loud, to a people standing at a mountain. And the first word, as Jews count them, is this. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." No rule. An introduction. Before anything is asked of you, you're told who is speaking and what they've already done for you. A relationship first, then everything else. Traditions number the ten a little differently. In the Jewish count, that opening sentence is the first word, and no other gods and no idols together are the second. Many Christian churches count them in other ways, Catholics and Lutherans one way, most other Protestants and the Orthodox another. Same text, different ways of dividing it. Then the tablets. An old midrash teaches they were five and five. The first tablet is between people and God: I am, no idols, the name, the Sabbath, and honor your parents, placed there because parents are partners in giving life. The second is between people: don't murder, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't lie in court, don't covet. And the midrash reads across the tablets: "thou shalt not murder" sits opposite "I am the LORD thy God," to teach that harming a person is harming the image of God. The Torah holds six hundred and thirteen commandments. Many teachers have seen these ten as the headings of all of them.

Most people pass the first few easily. Stop on the one that's hardest for you this week, probably the last, the wanting. Just notice it. The bell holds the time.
The Ten Words. Not ten rules in stone but ten sayings, beginning with an introduction: I am the one who brought you out. Thirteenth word.
Your line: ten sentences to build a life on. Today, pick one of the ten and let it be the only one you think about, all day. Day thirteen.

14.title: intention
14.hook: intention; the difference between saying and meaning

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ten Words, which begin with an introduction instead of a rule. Your line was ten sentences to build a life on. Which one did you carry? Day fourteen, the end of week two.

You've done this. You drive home and pull into the driveway, and you can't remember a single turn. Or you read a whole page, reach the bottom, and have no idea what it said. Or you say "love you" at the end of a phone call the way you'd say "bye." Your mouth did the job. You weren't there. Now imagine a tradition with words it says every day, morning and night, for a lifetime. The danger isn't forgetting them. It's saying them perfectly while you're somewhere else entirely. Judaism has a word for the thing that's missing. Today: intention.

segments.voice: Kavanah comes from a root that means to aim, to direct, to point something at a target. Intention is aiming your heart where your words are going. The Mishnah, discussing the Shema, the six words from day two, says that if a person directed their heart while reading, they have fulfilled the duty. It also remembers that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, just to direct their hearts. An hour of aiming, for a few minutes of prayer. And the Bible's clearest picture of kavanah is a woman named Hannah, praying at the sanctuary for a child. She speaks in her heart, the text says; only her lips move, and no sound comes out. The priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't. She's praying as hard as anyone ever has. The rabbis learned much of how to pray from her. The Talmud puts it in one line: the Merciful One wants the heart. But here's the honest part. The rabbis argued about whether a commandment done without intention still counts, and the discussion goes on for centuries. Many say yes, the act counts, but it's not the whole thing. And one teaching holds both sides together: do the good thing even when your heart isn't in it, because from doing it without the right intention, you come to do it with the right one. That's day twelve again, do first, with a promise attached. The meaning often shows up late. Keep the door open for it. This week you met Abraham, Jacob, tzedakah, the Exodus, Sinai, the Ten Words, and now the thing that makes any of them more than motions.

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Pick one short thing you say every day without thinking: thank you, good morning, love you, or, if you pray, the Shema. For the first part of the sit, just aim: who is it for, and what do you actually mean by it? Then say it once, slowly, meaning every word. The bell holds the time.
Kavanah. Intention: aiming your heart where your words and actions are going. Fourteenth word. Two weeks.
Your line: mean it. Today, catch one phrase you say on autopilot, and the next time you say it, stop half a second first and mean it. Day fourteen. Week two, done.
